claims.text: Greg Short asserts that prospects and counterparts on calls or in meetings have no ability to detect when you are having a bad day; the subjective internal state is invisible to the other party, so feeling bad is not a valid reason to defer a pitch, call, or meeting.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: high-stakes pitch, meeting, or sales call context
speaker is showing up in person or on a call (not async text)
bounded_by: Does not address written or async communication where emotional state may bleed through in word choice

claims.text: Greg Short asserts that consistent daily action (365 days per year without skipping) increases the probability of high-output days because the sheer volume of attempts produces more good-day outcomes than a competitor who skips when feeling bad; showing up more than the next person is the mechanism that shifts the percentage in your favor.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
claims.speaker_term: showing up more than the next guy
conditions: activity requiring daily execution (sales, client calls, pitches)
claims.mechanism: More total attempts in the sample produces more high-output days in absolute terms, regardless of the distribution of emotional states across those days; competitors who skip bad days have a smaller sample and therefore fewer peak-performance opportunities.

claims.text: Greg Short asserts that on days when a practitioner feels worst, the quality gap between their expected and actual performance is larger than on average days; the surprise of performing well on a bad day is disproportionately high, suggesting that self-assessment of readiness is systematically biased downward on low-energy days.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
claims.speaker_term: shocked at how good you do
conditions: practitioner who has baseline skill already developed
bounded_by: Claim is experience-report quality; no comparison group or measurement cited

practices.text: Execute high-stakes calls, pitches, and meetings every day regardless of how you feel; do not defer based on low energy or bad mood.
Show up and take action 365 days per year to increase your share of good-outcome days relative to competitors who skip when feeling low.
